source_text: Nos quidem neque expavescimus neque pertimescimus ea quae ab ignorantibus patimur, cum ad hanc sectam utique suscepta condicione eius pacti venerimus, ut etiam animas nostras auctorati in has pugnas accedamus, ea quae deus repromittit consequi optantes et ea quae diversae vitae comminatur pati timentes. Denique cum omni saevitia vestra concertamus etiam ultro erumpentes, magisque damnati quam absoluti gaudemus. Itaque hunc libellum non nobis timentes misimus, sed vobis et omnibus inimicis nostris, nedum amicis. Ita enim disciplina iubemur diligere inimicos quoque et orare pro iis qui nos persequuntur, ut haec sit perfecta et propria bonitas nostra, non communis. Amicos enim diligere omnium est, inimicos autem solorum Christianorum. Qui ergo dolemus de ignorantia vestra, et miseremur erroris humani, et futura prospicimus, et signa eorum cottidie intentari videmus, necesse est vel hoc modo erumpere ad proponenda vobis ea quae palam non vultis audire.
thought_title: Christians do not fear persecution but are compelled to speak
orientation: Tertullian opens his letter to Scapula by explaining why Christians endure suffering without fear and why he now writes to their enemies.
pass_a_gloss: We indeed neither dread nor fear those things which we suffer from ignorant people, since we have come to this faith at any rate having accepted the condition of its pact, so that we may go into these battles even with our souls sworn in, desiring to obtain the things which God promises and fearing to suffer the things which he threatens for the opposite life. Finally we fight with all your savagery even bursting forth of our own accord, and we rejoice more when condemned than when acquitted. Therefore we have sent this little book not fearing for ourselves, but for you and for all our enemies, not to mention friends. For so by the teaching we are commanded to love even our enemies and to pray for those who persecute us, so that this may be our perfect and proper goodness, not common. For to love friends belongs to all people, but to love enemies belongs only to Christians. Therefore we who grieve over your ignorance, and pity human error, and foresee the future, and see signs of it daily being brandished, must even in this way burst forth to set before you those things which you do not wish to hear openly.

choices.why: Glossary term; renders the Christian way of life as Tertullian adopts the outsider's term.
Glossary term; refers to the Christian teaching that commands love of enemies.
Conveys the gladiatorial metaphor of binding oneself by oath to enter the contest.
Reflects the diminutive form and the modest self-presentation of the letter.
Preserves the forceful, almost violent image of speaking out despite danger.
Keeps the contrast between the Christian life and the life that faces divine threats.

pass_b_english: We do not dread or fear greatly the things we suffer at the hands of the ignorant, since we came to this faith having accepted the terms of its covenant: we enter these contests sworn in, even with our souls, desiring to obtain what God has promised and fearing to suffer what He threatens against the opposite life. In fact, we contend with all your cruelty, even bursting forth of our own accord, and we rejoice more when condemned than when acquitted. So I have sent you this little book not because we are afraid for ourselves, but for you and for all our enemies—not to mention our friends. For our teaching commands us to love even our enemies and to pray for those who persecute us, so that this may be our perfect and distinctive goodness, not a common one. Loving friends is something everyone does; loving enemies belongs to Christians alone. Therefore, since we grieve over your ignorance, and pity human error, and foresee what is coming, and see the signs of it brandished against us daily, we must burst forth in this way at least, to set before you what you do not wish to hear openly.

problems.quote: even to the point of giving up our lives
problems.source_quote: ut etiam animas nostras auctorati in has pugnas accedamus
problems.why: Latin says they are authorized to bring their souls into the fight, not that they will sacrifice their lives.
problems.fix: we enter these contests, authorized to bring our souls into the fight
problems.ruling: auctorati means pledged/bound by oath, not 'giving up'; animas nostras accedamus means bring our souls into contests, not sacrifice them.

edits.old: we enter these contests sworn in, even to the point of giving up our lives
edits.new: we enter these contests sworn in, even with our souls

fixed: Changed 'even to the point of giving up our lives' to 'even with our souls' to match the source 'ut etiam animas nostras auctorati in has pugnas accedamus', which says they bring their souls into the fight, not that they sacrifice their lives.
